title: (title unknown)
bodyHtml:
Lopit is a language spoken by around 50,000 people in the Eastern Equatoria province of South Sudan. The Lopit people live in around 60 villages along the Lopit mountain range. They grow a range of crops and farm cattle, sheep and goats.

Below are some sentences in the Dorik dialect of Lopit. There is no official writing system for the language, but the spelling used here is what many Lopit people use. In Lopit, when a word-initial ‘e’ comes before an ‘o’ or a ‘u’, the ‘e’ is instead pronounced as an ‘o’.

eitiyena Iliwa aina
Iliwa teaches today.
eremo Lohidong waraga ho iguarit
Lohidong spears the paper with the pen.
oromo haboroni de mana
The big man digs in the field.
oboro habarani
The cattle owner is big.
eibongo haidoloni ho haromoni de lecari
The singer meets with the field hand at the dancehall.
eifuo Ihidong de leitiyenari
Ihidong cooks at the school.
efer hingohu de halu na haji
The dog lies at the back of the house.
eiyoma haromok de iferit
The field hands rest on the mat.
eramita wurre ho hingohu
The children play with the dog.

Translate the following sentences into Lopit and write them on the answer sheets.

questions.promptHtml: The big men dance with the shovel in the kitchen.
questions.partPrompt: Translate the following sentence into Lopit: The big men dance with the shovel in the kitchen.
questions.answerKey: eca haborok ho iromoit de leifuori

questions.partPrompt: Translate the following sentence into Lopit: The teacher sings.

questions.promptHtml: The cattle owners draw in the playground.
questions.partPrompt: Translate the following sentence into Lopit: The cattle owners draw in the playground.

hints.text: Start by lining up words that share a chunk of sound. Notice that the sentence about the singer contains haidoloni, and that the word for “dancehall”, lecari, looks related to something else in the data. Lopit builds many nouns out of verb roots by adding a prefix and sometimes a suffix.

There are four patterns to find: verbs begin with e- (spelled o- when the next vowel is o or u); “person who does X” nouns begin with ha-; place nouns begin with le- and end in -ri; instrument nouns begin with i- and end in -it. Also work out how singular and plural person-nouns differ, and which little word means “with” and which means “at/in/on”. Word order is verb first, then subject, then the rest.

Worked example not in the questions: “The field hand rests on the mat.” The verb “rest” appears as eiyoma, the singular of haromok is haromoni, and “on the mat” is de iferit, so the sentence is eiyoma haromoni de iferit. Build your answers the same way: verb, then subject noun with the right singular or plural ending, then the phrases with ho or de.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the word order

Compare oromo haboroni de mana “The big man digs in the field” with eramita wurre ho hingohu “The children play with the dog.” In both cases the first Lopit word is the verb, the second is the subject, and anything else comes afterwards. So Lopit puts the verb first: verb, subject, then object or prepositional phrase.

Two small words appear in front of nouns: ho means “with” (ho iguarit “with the pen”, ho hingohu “with the dog”) and de means “at / in / on” (de mana “in the field”, de lecari “at the dancehall”, de iferit “on the mat”).

Step 2: verbs all start with e-

Look at the first word of each sentence: eitiyena, eremo, oromo, oboro, eibongo, eifuo, efer, eiyoma, eramita. Every verb begins with e-, except that the introduction tells us a word-initial “e” is pronounced (and here written) “o” when the next vowel is “o” or “u”. That explains oromo (root romo “dig”) and oboro (root boro “be big”). So a verb is e- plus a root, with e becoming o before o or u.

Step 3: nouns are built from the same roots

Now hunt for the same roots inside the nouns. This is derivation — making new words out of a root by adding pieces:

  • People (“one who Xs”): ha- ... -ni. haboroni “big man” from boro “be big”; haidoloni “singer” from a root idolo “sing”; haromoni “field hand” from romo “dig”; habarani “cattle owner”.
  • Plural people: ha- ... -k. haromok “field hands” beside haromoni “field hand”. So the singular ending -ni is replaced by -k (and the root vowel before it is trimmed): haboroni gives haborok, habarani gives habarak.
  • Places: le- ... -ri. lecari “dancehall” from a root ca “dance”; leitiyenari “school” from itiyena “teach”; and by the same recipe leifuori “kitchen” from ifuo “cook”.
  • Instruments: i- ... -it. iferit “mat” from fer “lie” (the thing you lie on); iguarit “pen” from a root guar “write, draw”; so “shovel”, the thing you dig with, is i-romo-it = iromoit.

Step 4: build the three sentences

E1. “The big men dance with the shovel in the kitchen.” The verb “dance” uses the root ca found in lecari, so it is eca (the next vowel is a, so no change to o). “Big men” is the plural of haboroni: haborok. “With the shovel” is ho iromoit, and “in the kitchen” is de leifuori. Result: eca haborok ho iromoit de leifuori.

E2. “The teacher sings.” “Sing” comes from the root inside haidoloni “singer”, giving the verb eidolo (the vowel after e is i, so the e stays e). “Teacher” is a person-noun from “teach”: ha- plus the root plus -ni, giving haitayenani. Result: eidolo haitayenani.

E3. “The cattle owners draw in the playground.” “Draw” uses the root guar from iguarit “pen”; because the next vowel is u, the prefix e- is written o-, giving oguar. “Cattle owners” is the plural of habarani, namely habarak. “Playground” is a place-noun from ramita “play”: le-ramita-ri = leramitari, and “in” is de. Result: oguar habarak de leramitari.

Why this is neat

Lopit lets you spin a whole family of words off one root: from romo “dig” you get the verb oromo, the worker haromoni, the workers haromok, and the tool iromoit. Once you spot the four templates, you can build words the problem never showed you.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys copied verbatim from the official solution page (E1 eca haborok ho iromoit de leifuori; E2 eidolo haitayenani; E3 oguar habarak de leramitari). Parts are named after the booklet's own labels E1/E2/E3, one question each; ids E1.1, E2.1, E3.1. Points split 4/3/3 (official sheet gives no per-item breakdown for the 10 points). Note the official solution spells the teacher noun 'haitayenani' (with 'a', not 'i' as in 'eitiyena'); I added 'eidolo haitiyenani' as an accepted variant in case a solver regularizes the vowel — please confirm whether that leniency is desired. No figures.
